migrationNotes: Spine: one post in a yard with more and more ropes tied to it. Two pulls on a line, one rope tilted and split into components, two pulls at right angles combined into a resultant, then the rope that holds the post still.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): engr-forces-as-vectors-10, whose meaning (the resultant formula) is covered by the right-angles screen and the combine items.

lesson.title: Forces as vectors

lead.text: Take the post in the yard and start with the simplest arrangement, in which every rope runs along one straight line. Each pull has a size and a direction. We measure size in newtons, and because structures carry big loads we use kilonewtons (kN) instead, where 1 kN is 1,000 N, about the weight of a 100 kg load.

When two people pull the same way, their efforts team up and the sizes add. If one pulls with 6 kN and the other with 2 kN, the post feels 8 kN in that direction. If the second person pulls the opposite way instead, the two pulls fight each other and the post feels only the difference. Both cases are in the picture below.

afterFigure.text: Adding and subtracting is all we need while everything lies on one line, and that is also where the method stops. A rope that runs off at a slant cannot simply be added, because only part of its pull acts in any one direction. The next few screens deal with exactly that.

lead.text: Use what the last screen showed about pulls on a single line.

Now tie a rope to the top of the post and run it to a hook on a tall tree, some way off and higher up. The rope pulls the post towards the tree, and it also pulls the post upwards. One rope is doing two jobs at once.

We can describe that pull in two pieces. One piece acts across, along the horizontal, and the other acts up, along the vertical. The two pieces are at right angles to each other, and together they have exactly the effect of the original pull. Each piece is called a component of the force. A component is the same pull described in two parts, with nothing extra added. The picture below shows the pieces for two different slants.

afterFigure.text: The angle is measured up from the horizontal. The steeper the rope, the larger the upward piece and the smaller the sideways piece. A rope lying flat along the ground has no upward piece at all, and a rope pulling straight up has no sideways piece. The next screen turns this into numbers.

lead.text: To put numbers on the two pieces, draw the force as the sloping side of a right-angled triangle. The across piece lies along the horizontal side and the up piece along the upright side.

Trigonometry links those sides to the angle θ (theta), measured from the horizontal. The side that touches the angle carries the cosine of θ, so the across piece is F cos θ. The side opposite the angle carries the sine of θ, so the up piece is F sin θ. In both, F is the size of the whole force.

diagram.caption: The force is the sloping side. The across piece is F cos θ and the up piece is F sin θ. Use the buttons to compare 45° with a flatter 30°.

steps.headline: Split 20 kN at 60° above the horizontal into its two components.

lead.text: Here is the whole method for a steeper rope, with the reason for each line.

workedSteps.text: The horizontal side touches the angle, so use cosine.
The vertical side is opposite the angle, so use sine.
Check: the parts combine back to the original force.

steps.headline: Reading a slope instead of an angle

lead.text: Drawings of real structures often give a slope instead of an angle, such as a cable that rises 3 m for every 4 m it runs across. A slope like that is already a right-angled triangle, with the rise as the upright side and the run as the flat side. The cable itself is the sloping side.

Pythagoras gives its length: √(3² + 4²) = 5. The sine and cosine are only ratios of sides, so the up piece is the force times rise ÷ length and the across piece is the force times run ÷ length. A 10 kN pull on that cable has an up piece of 10 × 3/5 = 6 kN and an across piece of 10 × 4/5 = 8 kN, with no calculator needed.

afterFigure.text: The shortcut works whenever the sides come out as whole numbers, as with 3, 4, 5 or 5, 12, 13. When they do not, fall back on the angle and your calculator.

steps.headline: A 5 kN cable pull runs along a line that rises 3 m for every 4 m across. Find its vertical component.

lead.text: Same method as the last screen, now on a smaller pull.

workedSteps.text: Find the long side of the slope triangle.
The vertical share is the rise over the long side.
Multiply the pull by that share, in kN.

lead.text: Splitting a force is half the job. The other half is putting forces back together. Suppose one person pulls the post east with 8 kN and another pulls it north with 15 kN. The post feels a single combined pull, called the resultant: the one force that does the work of all the others.

Forces on one line just add. These two are at right angles, so adding their sizes would overstate the result. Instead, treat the two pulls as the sides of a right-angled triangle. The resultant is the long side. If Rx is the pull across and Ry the pull up, Pythagoras gives R = √(Rx² + Ry²). For our post the squares add up to 64 + 225 = 289, and the square root of 289 is 17 kN.

afterFigure.text: Notice that 17 kN is less than 8 + 15 = 23 kN. Two pulls at right angles partly pull in different directions, so they never team up as well as two pulls along one line. This is the same triangle we used to split a force, read in the other direction.

lead.text: The two pulls meet at right angles, so treat them as the sides of a triangle.

Back at the post, suppose we want it to stay perfectly still. Then the ropes must cancel each other out, so that their resultant is zero. A body in that state is in equilibrium. Engineers write the condition as ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0, where Σ (sigma) means “the sum of”: the across pieces add to zero and the up pieces add to zero.

To check, they first draw the post on its own, with every force that acts on it as an arrow and nothing else. No ground, no tree, no people, only arrows. This sketch is called a free-body diagram. Only forces acting on the body belong on it. The post pulls on the rope too, but that force acts on the rope, so it stays off the post's drawing.

afterFigure.text: Drawn tip to tail, the arrows of a body in equilibrium close up into a shape with no gap, because the last arrow ends exactly where the first began. That gives a quick way to find a missing force. Add up the ones you know, and the missing force has the same size as their resultant and points the opposite way.

blocks.text: Picture a strong post in the corner of a yard with a rope tied to its top. One person pulls on the rope and the post leans a little. A second person joins in on the same rope and it leans further. Nothing surprising yet, since two pulls the same way make a bigger pull.

Now a third person takes a second rope and pulls from the side. Someone else runs a rope from the top of the post down to a ring in the ground, so it slants. Each rope pulls in its own direction, and the post feels all of them at once. Bridges, cranes and roof frames face the same situation, with cables and bars pulling at every angle.

This lesson follows the post as the ropes pile on. We start with two pulls along a line and then tilt one, which leads to splitting a slanted pull into two straight ones. After that, pulls at right angles go back together, and the last job is finding the rope that would hold the post perfectly still.

diagram.alt: A post standing on the ground. First, two pulls on one rope along the same line add to one bigger pull. Second, three ropes tied to the top of the post pull in three different directions.
diagram.caption: Two pulls on one rope team up. Ropes at different angles each pull in their own direction. Use the buttons to compare the two.

intro.promise: By the end you'll split a slanted force into two straight parts and combine forces at right angles.

recap.keyIdea: A slanted force splits into an across part and an up part. Forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras, and a body in balance has forces that cancel.

blocks.text: Back at the post, you split 10 kN at 30° into 8.66 kN across and 5.00 kN up, and read a 5 kN pull on a 3 in 4 slope as a 3-4-5 triangle with a 3 kN upward part. You combined 3 kN and 4 kN at right angles into 5 kN, not 7 kN, and found that a 6 kN and an 8 kN pull need a 10 kN pull the opposite way to hold a ring still.

recap.nextHook: Pulls also turn things, as a hand on a spanner turns a bolt, and the next lesson works out what decides how hard a push twists.

questions.prompt: Two people pull a trolley along a straight rail in the same direction, one with 3 kN and one with 4 kN. What is the combined pull, in kN?
hints: Both pull the same way. Do the pulls help each other or fight?
Forces along one line simply combine.
Put the two pulls together.
questions.onCorrect: 7 kN. Pulls along one line in the same direction just add. Pulls at an angle need more care.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 4 − 3. They pull the same way, so they work together.
That multiplies the pulls. Forces on one line combine by adding.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pulls act on one line in the same direction, so they add: 3 + 4 = 7 kN.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the vertical component of a force F at angle θ above the horizontal?
hints: Which side of the triangle is opposite the angle?
questions.onCorrect: The vertical side is opposite θ, so it is F sin θ. The side next to the angle gets the cosine.

misconceptions.feedback: F cos θ is the horizontal part, the side that touches the angle.
tan θ is a ratio of two sides, not a share of the force. A component is F times sin θ or cos θ.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: F sin θ. The vertical component is the side opposite θ: F sin θ.

questions.prompt: A 10 kN force acts at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal component, in kN, to two decimal places.
hints: The horizontal side of the triangle is next to the 30° angle.
Next to the angle means cosine: the share is F cos θ.
Calculate 10 × cos 30° and round to two decimal places.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal component = 10 cos 30° = 8.660 kN, which rounds to 8.66 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 8.66 kN. Next to the angle means cosine: the horizontal part is F cos θ.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 10 sin 30°, the vertical part. The horizontal side touches the angle, so use cosine.
That is the whole force. Only part of an angled force acts across.

questions.prompt: Why is the horizontal part 20 cos 60° and not 20 sin 60°?
hints: Which side of the triangle touches the 60° angle?
questions.onCorrect: Cosine goes with the side that touches the angle, whatever its size.

misconceptions.feedback: At 60° the cosine is the smaller one. The choice depends on which side touches the angle.
The angle is measured from the horizontal here, so the horizontal side touches it.

choices.label: The horizontal side touches the angle, so it is the cosine share.
Because cos is always the larger of the two.
Because 60° is measured from the vertical.

acceptedIdeas: The horizontal side touches the angle, so it is the cosine share.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The horizontal side touches the angle, so it is the cosine share.. The horizontal side touches the angle, so it takes the cosine.

hints: Which side of the slope triangle is the rise?
The vertical share is rise over long side.
Multiply the pull by that share.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope triangle 3–4–5 gives sin θ = 3/5, so the vertical component is 5 × 3/5 = 3 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 3 kN: the pull times rise over long side. Any slope triangle gives the shares without a calculator.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the horizontal part: the run over the long side. The vertical part uses the rise.
That is the whole pull. Only a fraction of it acts upward.
The share is over the long side of the triangle, not over the run.

questions.prompt: Which gives the size of the resultant of perpendicular components Rx and Ry?
hints: Think of the two components as the sides of a right-angled triangle.
questions.onCorrect: The resultant is the long side of the triangle the components make, so Pythagoras applies.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding the sizes only works for forces on one line. At right angles the resultant is shorter.
Multiplying gives units of kN squared, not a force.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: √(Rx² + Ry²). The resultant is the hypotenuse: √(Rx² + Ry²).

questions.prompt: A pin carries 3 kN acting horizontally and 4 kN acting vertically. Find the size of their resultant in kN.
hints: The forces are at right angles, so their sizes do not simply add.
Use Pythagoras on the two components.
Calculate √(3² + 4²).
questions.onCorrect: 5 kN. Square, add, root: the resultant is the long side of the force triangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes, which only works for forces on one line. These are at right angles.
That is the sum of the squares. Take the square root to get back to a force.

questions.prompt: A ring is held by 6 kN along +x and 8 kN along +y. What size, in kN, must a third force have to keep the ring in equilibrium?
hints: Equilibrium needs the sum of all forces to be zero.
The third force cancels the resultant of the other two.
Calculate √(6² + 8²).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The third force must cancel the resultant of the first two: √(6² + 8²) = 10 kN, pointing opposite it.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN, pointing opposite the resultant. A closed force polygon means equilibrium.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes. They are at right angles, so find their resultant first.
That is the difference of the sizes. The forces are at right angles, not opposed.

questions.prompt: Forces of 12 kN along +x and 5 kN along +y act on the pin of a gusset plate. Find the size of their resultant in kN.
hints: Treat the two forces as perpendicular components.
Square each, add, then take the square root.
Calculate √(144 + 25).
questions.onCorrect: 13 kN. At right angles, square, add and take the root.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. At right angles they combine by Pythagoras.
That is the sum of the squares. The last step is the square root.

questions.prompt: A 26 kN force acts along a line that rises 5 m for every 12 m across. Find its vertical component in kN.
hints: Find the long side of a triangle with sides 5 and 12.
The vertical share is rise over long side.
Calculate 26 × 5 ÷ 13.
questions.onCorrect: 10 kN: the force times rise over long side, the long side being 13.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the horizontal part, the run over the long side. The vertical part uses the rise.
That is the whole force. Only a share of it acts upward.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope triangle 5–12–13 gives sin θ = 5/13, so the vertical component is 26 × 5/13 = 10 kN.

questions.prompt: A lamp hangs from two cables. Its free-body diagram isolates the lamp. Which force belongs on that diagram?

acceptedIdeas: The pull of each cable on the lamp
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pull of each cable on the lamp. The cable pulls act on the lamp, so they belong on its diagram.

choices.label: The pull of each cable on the lamp

questions.onCorrect: A free-body diagram holds only forces acting on the isolated body: here the lamp's weight and the two cable pulls.

misconceptions.feedback: That force acts on the ceiling, not on the lamp. Only forces on the isolated body belong.
The ceiling's weight acts on the ceiling. It does not act on the lamp.
